strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: exact empirical 0-1 loss minimization for low-dimensional linear classifiers could provide useful models and benchmarks for surrogate objectives.
The explicit Haskell implementation, including linear algebra routines, makes the proposed enumeration and loss-bound pruning procedures inspectable.
weaknesses: The implemented loss contradicts the stated objective. Equation (1) defines sign(0)=0, making boundary points misclassified, whereas loss01 assigns them zero loss regardless of their labels. For one-dimensional points x=(1,2) with labels (-1,+1), every enumerated boundary has Equation (1) loss one, while a threshold at 1.5 achieves zero. A perturbation could potentially recover the intended labeling under suitable assumptions, but no such classifier-construction step is supplied.

The claimed O(N^D) worst-case runtime is contradicted by the algorithm on pages 7–8. Without pruning, each of the binomial(N,D) candidates evaluates its entire prefix when constructed and every subsequent point, totaling N·binomial(N,D)=Theta(N^(D+1)) point evaluations for fixed D. Incremental updates do not remove this factor of N, and pruning provides no demonstrated worst-case improvement.

The correctness proof contains an invalid inference. Appendix A argues that greater Hamming distance from an optimal cell's predictions implies greater loss against the true labels. Optimality does not establish this monotonic relationship. Consequently, the supplied proof does not justify the central vertex-selection argument.

The implementation has additional failures even on inputs in general position. In two dimensions, points (1,0), (2,0), and (0,1) are in general position, but fitw encounters a singular matrix for the first pair because its fixed-intercept parameterization cannot represent their boundary through the origin; rotatePivot has no terminating singular-case handling. Furthermore, the fixed 1e-8 tolerance can produce falsely optimal losses: distinct one-dimensional points (1,1+1e-9,1+2e-9), labeled (-1,+1,-1), are all treated as boundary points and receive reported loss zero, although every linear threshold makes at least one error.

The claim of the first provably polynomial-time exact algorithm is inadequately established. Classical hyperplane-arrangement construction and dichotomy enumeration, including results cited by the manuscript, already provide a route to polynomial-time exact optimization in fixed dimension. The paper does not adequately distinguish its contribution from that route or substantiate its claimed complexity improvement.

The evaluation cannot substantiate the central claims. Table 1 contains error counts for only five small, low-dimensional datasets, with no runtime or memory measurements, comparisons against exact solvers, independent optimality verification, or pruning ablations. Preprocessing, baseline tuning, and train/test protocols are unspecified. Lower reported empirical loss therefore establishes neither computational efficiency nor superior predictive performance, and does not support the proposed replacement of SVMs in high-stakes applications.
